Even if you already have the equipment for the pickling and canning (jars, stockpot, maybe a pressure cooker depending) it will still take time too.

One tip I can give is to try buying your jalapenos from a restaurant supply store or maybe a mexican grocery. If you use bulk amounts anyway you may as well buy in bulk.

I live in a condo, and still grow some of my own. If you've got a balcony you can fit a surprising amount of plants, especially if you use vertical space too. Even without a balcony you can still do windowsill gardens for herbs or a few jalapeno plants. Or you can toss a full spectrum lightbulb in a closet and pretend like you grow pot.

Or if your condo has any sort of yard space talk with your association about setting up a small garden there, or even a big garden for the whole building.
I do have a small patio outside. I just assumed that I don't have space for it, but I should try. Do you think May is too late to start planting anything?
From seed, way too late, but any home improvement store will have plants already started that will grow just fine.
Just keep in mind that any home grown jalapenos are way hotter than store bought ones. The store bought ones have been bred for speed of growth and extended shelf life at the expense of flavor.

Highly unlikely. When you're paying for fresh jalapenos, you're paying a premium because of the transport costs of fresh produce. This is an expense that the pickled manufacturers save, and pass on to you. Furthermore, pickled jalapenos are often of lower grade than fresh, since their shape, color, and texture isn't nearly as important. More savings passed on to you. There are very few produce related items that are cheaper to do at home. Doing it at home is usually spending a premium in order to get a better quality, not to save money.

Absolutely, with a catch.

The speed of light is not really a speed limit. What happens near the speed of light is that time, as is commonly understood, starts to do really strange things. You can travel millions of light years in a single human life - and really as far as you want. We can never perceive anything as going faster than the speed of light, but from your own perspective (or for instance, from those aboard the ship) you can continue to accelerate with no 'speed limit'. The universe 'cheats' to keep things within the speed of light from your perspective such as making time for you start to slow down (1 second for you might be 10 seconds or even 10 years for a relatively at rest observer) and distances themselves will begin to physically contract, but the net result is that you get to travel distances far beyond what you could in the lifetime of a single human.

Here some examples of the math are worked out. In particular if we can build a craft capable of accelerating at 1g per second then:

  • In 3.6 years you can travel 4.3 light years.

  • In 6.6 years you can travel 27 light years.

  • In 20 years you can travel 30,000 light years.

  • In 28 years you can travel 2,000,000 light years.

And so on. These values also account for slowing down. Half the time is spent accelerating and then half the time is spent decelerating to finally come to rest at the final destination.

This is not a theory (in the colloquial sense). The math is used for instance to synchronize GPS satellites with earth. They rely on extremely high precision atomic clocks yet travel fast enough that relativistic effects make their clocks tick, from our perspective, faster than clocks on earth do. If these relativistic effects were not accounted for GPS errors would accumulate to the tune of 10 kilometers a day!

Essentially our universe allows you to press a 'fast forward' button if you yourself meet certain conditions such as traveling sufficiently rapidly relative to something else or being within the vicinity of a body with a sufficiently large gravitational pull. Some people may not realize the science in the movie Interstellar, for instance, was based on our actual universe. The catch is that time itself does genuinely change. You may go 30,000 light years in 20 years - but back on Earth 30,000 years will actually have passed. By the time you reach your destination everybody and everything you knew will be long since dead. Although in some mind bending 'paradoxes' if we send a ship off at 1g and then later on develop and build a system that can accelerate even faster then you might make it to the other galaxy only to find that people born hundreds of years after you left are already there... Gotta love our universe.

Okay, to be clear when I say "perspective" - I am not talking about sleight of hands, or magic tricks. The observer, and the relativistic particles experience different realities simultaneously. And both realities are "real." The increase in mass is an observer effect. What this means is that we see the mass increase and in every single possible way we could interact and deal with that particle - it will have a greater mass from the perspective of the observer. However, from the perspective of the particle itself - it's an entirely different story. There is no mass increase.

For another example of this consider time. Imagine we have a particle that's normally stable for only 1 second 'in the wild.' We know that anytime that particle comes into existence, it decays in exactly 1 second. Now we create a scenario where that particle is created in a high energy situation where it's being accelerated to the point of having a time dilation factor of 1000. How long would it take it to decay? 1000 seconds. There's no magic - just our universe doing it's incredibly bizarre thing. Although this is from an observer perspective. If somehow we were able to 'be' that particle, it would indeed have decayed after 1 second. Two simultaneous realities, both experiencing radically different views of the same event, both right. Our universe is a fun place, eh?

No, you're not mistaken but you're not getting the nuance. An object's mass is observed to increase as its speed increases. In particular as its speed approaches c its mass is observed to approach infinity. This is what causes the massive in energy needed for an observed body to accelerate closer and closer to c. But again this is all what we observe. From the perspective of something that is accelerating basic newtonian mechanics continues to work exactly the same whether you've thrusted 1 times or 1 trillion times beforehand.

Imagine we could stick a little thruster on a particle. We'd observe each thrust, later on, to begin producing less and less acceleration. It'd require the same amount of energy as we currently expend. But from the perspective of that particle, it'd be generating just as much thrust each and every time the thruster fired. The big difference is that the particle's perception of time, and our perception of time, begin to diverge dramatically as it relativistically approaches c relative to us. For instance it will be going around the accelerator far more times than we will have observed it going around the accelerator. The increase in the particle's observed lifetime is us 'catching up' to the time that it has already experienced.
